newsitem.title: FRANCE: French left loses ground one year before election.
newsitem.headline: French left loses ground one year before election.

text.p: Support for France's Socialist-led opposition has slipped as conservative Prime Minister Alain Juppe slowly recovers in public esteem, an opinion poll published on Wednesday showed.

The BVA poll for Paris Match magazine, published exactly a year before a general election is due, found that Juppe's centre-right coalition would beat left-wing parties headed by Socialist leader Lionel Jospin if the vote were held now.

But a big majority of voters remain dissatisfied with the way France is run, the poll showed. Only 20 percent of those asked were satisfied with the government, a one-point drop from February. Seventy-six percent were unhappy.
Jospin's popularity fell by two points to 41 percent but support for the left in general eroded more sharply.

If elections were held today, the left would win 38 percent compared with 42.5 percent a month ago. Support for the centre-right rose 3.5 points to 40 percent, with the extreme-right National Front up one point at 13 percent.
President Jacques Chirac's approval rating was unchanged at 39 percent. Juppe's support rose from 27 to 29 percent.
The pollsters questioned 1,018 adults on March 13-15 on the popularity of political leaders. For the election simulation, they sampled 1,740 registered voters between March 3 and 8.
A second poll for the weekly L'Express also confirmed a steady revival in Chirac's and Juppe's standings in recent months, despite record unemployment.

The Gallup survey showed that 44 percent approved of Chirac's actions as president, up from 36 percent in the last comparable poll in January. The percentage of those who disapproved fell from 52 to 47 percent.
Juppe's approval rating climbed from 30 to 37 percent in the survey of 946 people on March 13 and 14. The number of those disapproving slid from 66 to 57 percent.
